The novel opens with a wealthy merchant, Nikolai's description of his meeting with several gentlemen at a party in Moscow after 24 hours without sleep. He explains that although he had only been there to meet an old friend and acquaintance, once present, the men began talking about women. Nikolai becomes disturbed due to their stories about women, and he attempts to make peace by relating stories of his own experience as well. A German doctor recounted his life-long love affair with a woman who was married off to another man; her husband allowed them conjugal visits until they eventually fled Europe together. A young Russian officer related how his father paid dearly to educate him but then gave away all of his money for an exquisite mistress. Two more told stories similar tales before Nikolay decided it would be best if everyone stop sharing stories. Shortly after, everybody went home leaving Nikoliy alone with two guests still asleep beside him; when they awake, the men realize Nikolay’s wife has also attended without his knowledge.

Some time later on route via carriage to St Petersburg, Nikolai expresses some frustration over not being able to enjoy himself fully during intercourse with his mistress or even find satisfaction by masturbating. His companion assures him he merely needs to practice more control and promises to teach him proper self-control through meditation. With this advice, Nikolai resolves never again to touch any other women sexually apart from his wife or feel lustful thoughts towards anyone else out of respect. To demonstrate his resolve, Nikolay cuts of one of his hands. Once in St Petersburgh, Nikolay makes frequent use of his dagger in private against his arm causing it bleed heavily onto bed sheets where he sleeps. During meals, he frequently threatens suicide to impress upon others his strong willpower.

The novel follows the story of Emma, a young woman struggling to find her place in the world after graduating from college. She moves back home to her childhood house and takes a job at a local café. As she navigates through daily life interactions with friends, family, co-workers, and customers, Emma begins to realize that finding purpose is not as clear cut as she thought.

Her days blend together filled with routine tasks mixed up with random conversations and moments of joy or frustration. It's during these simple yet profound experiences where she starts questioning what truly defines her existence. Meanwhile, an unexpected friendship develops when one of her regular customers reveals he’s dealing with his own existential crisis. Together, they embark on a journey exploring their surroundings, relationships and deepening the conversation around Life itself. With each passing day, Emma learns more about herself and gains new perspectives, leading her to question whether happiness can ever be found or if it has always been here all along.

In the field of person re-identification (re-ID), most existing methods assume a closed-set scenario, where the identities of query persons are guaranteed to appear in the gallery dataset. However, in reality, re-ID often needs to be deployed in an open-set scenario, where the gallery dataset may contain unknown or unseen persons. This paper addresses the problem of open-set person re-ID and proposes a novel method to effectively handle the challenges of open-set recognition. The proposed method combines a feature-level embedding network with a classification-based open-set recognition module. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-set person re-ID. The findings of this study contribute to the development of more robust and accurate person re-ID systems in real-world applications.

> Point clouds are widely used in 3D scene understanding, but they have not been fully explored in semantic segmentation tasks due to their sparsity and irregular structure. In this work, we propose an end-to-end deep learning framework that can directly process point cloud data without any preprocessing or postprocessing steps. Our method takes as input raw points with no prior information about the object classes present in the scene. It then learns to flow semantic labels through these points by using a novel convolutional neural network architecture called PointFlow. We show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two challenging datasets (NYUv2 and ScanNet) while being significantly faster than other approaches.

> We study principal sub-manifolds in Riemannian manifolds, which are defined as those that admit an action by a Lie group with compact stabilizers and whose orbit space has finite volume. In particular we show that every closed manifold admits such a structure if it satisfies certain topological conditions. This generalizes results of Gromov on hyperbolic structures and of Thurston on geometric structures. Our main tool is a new version of the Borel density theorem due to Cheeger and Colding.

Segmenter: Transformer for Semantic Segmentation

In this paper, we present Segmenter, a novel deep learning model for semantic segmentation that utilizes a transformer architecture. The transformer architecture has shown great success in natural language processing tasks, but its effectiveness in image segmentation has not been fully explored. We propose a transformer-based model for semantic segmentation that can effectively capture long-range dependencies between pixels and improve the accuracy of segmentation.

Our model consists of an encoder-decoder architecture, where the encoder processes the input image and generates a sequence of feature vectors, and the decoder generates the segmentation mask based on these feature vectors. The transformer architecture is used in both the encoder and decoder to process the sequence of feature vectors. We also introduce a novel attention mechanism that allows the model to focus on the most relevant regions of the image during segmentation.

We evaluate our model on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and speed. Our model is also able to handle complex scenes with multiple objects and backgrounds, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications.

Overall, our work demonstrates the effectiveness of transformer architectures in image segmentation and paves the way for further research in this area.

In this paper, we propose a novel method for constructing a non-negative low rank and sparse graph with data-adaptive features. Our approach leverages the strengths of non-negative matrix factorization and sparse graph representation to create a robust and efficient graph model that can accurately capture the complex relationships between data points.

The proposed method consists of two main stages. First, we use a non-negative matrix factorization technique to decompose the data matrix into two low-rank matrices, which capture the underlying structure of the data. We then use these matrices to construct a sparse graph, where each node represents a data point and the edges represent the similarity between the data points.

The key innovation of our method is the use of data-adaptive features, which are learned from the data itself. These features are used to weight the edges in the graph, allowing the model to selectively focus on the most important relationships between data points. This results in a graph that is both sparse and informative, making it well-suited for tasks such as clustering, classification, and dimensionality reduction.

We evaluate our method on several real-world datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art graph construction methods. The results show that our method outperforms the competition in terms of both computational efficiency and accuracy. We also demonstrate the versatility of our method by applying it to a variety of applications, including image segmentation, text classification, and recommender systems.

Overall, our paper makes an important contribution to the field of graph construction and demonstrates the power of non-negative low rank and sparse graph representation with data-adaptive features. The proposed method has broad applications in data analysis, machine learning, and related fields, and we expect it to be of interest to researchers and practitioners working in these areas.

Deep Geodesic Learning for Segmentation and Anatomical Landmarking

In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning framework for segmentation and anatomical landmarking of medical images. Our approach is based on geodesic learning, which involves learning a smooth and continuous mapping between the input image and a target image. We extend this idea to the deep learning setting by using a deep neural network to learn the mapping. We also introduce a novel loss function that encourages the learned mapping to preserve the anatomical structure of the image. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several medical image segmentation and landmarking tasks, and show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

Using a simple phenomenological model, we have studied the spin reorientation transition (SRT) in (Ga,Mn)As. We have calculated the free energy as a function of the Mn spin orientation angle theta and the tetragonal anisotropy parameter K. We have found that there is a critical value of the tetragonal anisotropy parameter, K_c, below which the SRT does not occur. For K>K_c, the SRT occurs at a critical value of the Mn spin orientation angle, theta_c. We have also calculated the critical exponents associated with the SRT.

The paper presents a novel automatic color image segmentation method based on a square elemental region-based seeded region growing and merging algorithm. The proposed method utilizes a square element as the basic unit of segmentation, which enables the algorithm to capture complex and irregular object boundaries in a more accurate and efficient manner. The algorithm consists of two stages: region growing and region merging. In the region growing stage, the algorithm starts with a set of seed points and iteratively grows the regions by expanding the boundaries of adjacent squares until a specified stopping criterion is met. In the region merging stage, the algorithm combines adjacent regions that share a common boundary to form a larger region. The proposed method has been evaluated on a standard dataset, and the experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency compared to existing algorithms.

This academic paper deals with the investigation of secure degrees of freedom (DoF) and jammer scaling law for multiuser wireless networks using the opportunistic jammer selection (OJS) technique. The communication system utilizes OJS to enhance secrecy communication by exploiting multiuser diversity. The paper begins by deriving the secure DoF for such a communication system wherein secure DoF is characterized as the pre-log factor of the secrecy capacity. The results indicate that adding more friendly jammers improves secure DoF, however, its value saturates due to the limited channel spatial degrees of freedom. Subsequently, a jammer scaling law that maximizes secure DoF per jammer is derived. Simulations confirm that the proposed system not only significantly enhances the secure DoF but also reduces computational complexity with increasing numbers of eavesdroppers. The paper provides valuable insights towards developing more secure and efficient wireless communication systems.

We evaluate our approach on the Omnidirectional Image Segmentation Benchmark (OISB) dataset. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OISB dataset.

Neutron stars, the densest known objects in the universe, provide a unique opportunity to study extreme energy density matter. In this paper, we review the various ways in which neutron stars can act as probes of this exotic form of matter. We discuss the properties of the high-density equation of state, the structure and composition of neutron stars, and the astrophysical observations that can be used to constrain these properties. We also explore the implications of recent observations, such as gravitational wave detections and the measurement of neutron star radii, for our understanding of extreme energy density matter. Finally, we discuss future prospects for studying neutron stars and the potential insights they can provide into the fundamental physics of dense matter.

This academic paper investigates thermalization, a phenomenon in which small random perturbations of dynamical systems reach equilibrium over time. Using mathematical models and simulations, we analyze how these perturbations evolve and dissipate energy within the system. Our findings suggest that thermalization occurs more rapidly when the perturbation is distributed evenly across the system's degrees of freedom. Additionally, we observe that the rate of thermalization depends on the specific properties of the dynamical system being studied. Overall, our research contributes to a better understanding of thermalization processes in complex systems and has potential applications in various fields such as physics, engineering, and finance.

In this paper, we present a numerical investigation of the tailoring of magnetic dipole radiation through the use of substrates. By simulating the interaction between a magnetic dipole and various types of substrates, we demonstrate the ability to control the radiation pattern, spectral intensity, and polarization properties of the emitted radiation. We show that the substrate can be used to manipulate the magnetic dipole's radiation in a variety of ways, including enhancing or suppressing certain frequencies, changing the direction of radiation, and creating complex radiation patterns. Our results have important implications for the design of magnetic dipole-based devices, such as antennas, sensors, and energy harvesters, and open up new possibilities for tailoring electromagnetic radiation in a variety of applications.

This paper presents a real-time high-performance semantic image segmentation method for urban street scenes. The method incorporates several key techniques, including dilated convolutions, atrous spatial pyramid pooling, and skip connections, to improve the segmentation performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and speed. The method achieves real-time performance on a standard GPU, making it suitable for various applications such as autonomous driving and urban planning.

In this study, we explore the potential of combining CNN-based feature extraction with random forest classifiers to improve the accuracy and efficiency of image classification systems. We study the problem of avoiding patterns in random permutations. Given a permutation $\pi$ of length $n$, a pattern $\sigma$ is said to occur in $\pi$ if there is a subsequence of $\pi$ that is in the same relative order as $\sigma$. The avoidance probability $P(\pi,\sigma)$ is the probability that a permutation $\pi$ of length $n$ does not contain $\sigma$ as a pattern. We prove that, for any fixed pattern $\sigma$, the avoidance probability $P(\pi,\sigma)$ tends to 1 as $n$ tends to infinity. This result is best possible in the sense that, for any $\epsilon>0$, there is a pattern $\sigma$ such that $P(\pi,\sigma)<1-\epsilon$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Automata: an approach to the understanding of computational systems in an evolutionary approach.

The emergence of new types of machines in our world has been a major, if not the major, subject of scientific speculation. Evolution describes a process by which organisms change through natural selection and variation. Although scientists have long understood that species will evolve, they did not understand the processes which lead to the emergence of new classes of systems. Some models of evolution imply that new, new, new, and different types of machines may arise and reproduce. Furthermore, although many scientific theories explain the emergence of new types of systems, they were based on a single-stage of evolution, often a single process. This paper introduces the concept of quantitative automatization. It analyzes the evolution and evolution of a binary reinforcement learner, QRP, as it uses probabilistic semantics. QRP is a model of a simple, but widely exploited, model of human decision-making. This paper shows that the process of the evolution of the system is equivalent to the process required to explain human decision-making. The conclusion of this analysis leads the authors to a novel account of the emergence and evolution of quantitative automata which, along with other approaches to the study of natural language, may provide the ultimate foundation for our understanding of computational systems.

Atrous convolution (AC) is an algorithm that can be used to extract semantic information from images, and it has been widely applied in image segmentation tasks such as object detection and face recognition. However, AC has several limitations, including its high computational cost and limited ability to recover semantic features from noisy data. We propose a new method based on a novel combination of AC-based methods and deep learning techniques that allows us to overcome these limitations by using a more efficient implementation of AC. Our approach combines two different approaches: (i) a fast and flexible implementation of AC with a novel feature extraction strategy; and (ii) a deep neural network architecture that learns to extract semantic features from noisy data. The resulting system achieves state-of-the-art performance on both object detection and face recognition tasks.

As she becomes increasingly adept at doling out empty compliments, Lily begins to lose touch with her authentic self.

We introduce a novel approach to study protein aggregation, based on statistical mechanics. Our method is based on the idea that proteins are subject to a large number of interactions, and that these interactions can be represented by a lattice model. We introduce a generalized master equation that describes the time evolution of the protein conformational space, and use it to derive a set of self-consistent equations that describe the equilibrium properties of the system. Our approach allows us to study the effects of different interaction types, and to determine the conditions under which protein aggregation occurs. We find that protein aggregation is a multi-step process, and that the initial steps are determined by local interactions between proteins. The later stages of aggregation are determined by global properties of the system, such as the total number of proteins and the average size of the aggregates. Our approach provides a quantitative understanding of protein aggregation, and can be used to predict the effects of different interactions on the aggregation process.

We present an unsupervised learning algorithm that learns to classify images into different categories based on their feature vectors, and we show how this can be used in image segmentation tasks such as object detection or face recognition. We use our method to train a classifier that predicts whether an image belongs to one of several classes (e.g., faces, animals, cars) using only unlabeled training data. Our approach has been trained with over 1 million labeled examples and achieves accuracy rates of up to 80% on the MNIST dataset. The results are comparable to state-of-the-art methods for object classification, which typically require tens of thousands of labeled examples.

In this witty and satirical novel, set in late 16th-century England, a young woman named Epicoene is determined to buck societal norms and live life on her own terms. Born into a wealthy family, Epicoene has always been expected to marry well and live a quiet, respectable life. But she has other plans.

Despite her parents' best efforts to find her a suitable husband, Epicoene remains resolute in her determination to remain unmarried and silent. She refuses to speak, communicating only through gestures and facial expressions, much to the frustration of those around her. Her silence becomes both a source of fascination and a subject of ridicule among the townspeople.

As Epicoene navigates the complexities of high society, she meets a cast of colorful characters who challenge her beliefs and test her resolve. There's the charming but duplicitous suitor who tries to win her hand in marriage; the outspoken and independent actress who becomes her closest friend; and the wise old philosopher who teaches her about the power of language and communication.

Throughout the novel, Epicoene must confront the various ways in which women are silenced and marginalized by society. She witnesses the plight of women who are forced into marriages they don't want, subjected to physical abuse, and denied access to education and economic opportunities. As she struggles to make her voice heard, Epicoene begins to question whether her silence is truly a form of empowerment or simply a means of avoiding conflict.

With its sharp dialogue and clever wordplay, this novel pokes fun at the hypocrisies of gender roles and social conventions while also celebrating the strength and resilience of women. Through Epicoene's journey, we see that even in the face of adversity, one can find their voice and make a meaningful impact on the world.

Gastric histopathology image segmentation is an important task in computer-aided diagnosis of gastric diseases, as it allows for accurate identification and quantification of different regions of interest in the stomach. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to gastric histopathology image segmentation using a hierarchical conditional random field (HCRF). Our method leverages the rich contextual information present in histopathology images by modeling the joint probability distribution of pixel labels across multiple scales.

Experiments on a large dataset of gastric histopathology images demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to traditionalCRF models. We also perform a thorough analysis of the contributions of different components of our HCRF model, providing insights into the role of contextual information in gastric histopathology image segmentation.

Our work has important implications for the development of computer-aided diagnosis systems for gastric diseases, and demonstrates the potential of HCRFs for segmenting complex histopathology images.

The first approach uses a technique called "normalizing flow", which allows us to normalize the data before performing the classification task. The second approach uses a technique known as "unsupervised learning", which allows us to learn the features of the training data without any prior knowledge about the labels. This paper continues the study of lifting representations of finite reductive groups. In particular, we focus on the explicit conorms of these lifting representations. We provide a general formula for computing the conorms, which allows us to explicitly determine the conorms for various finite reductive groups. We also establish several interesting properties of the conorms, such as their relation to the central characters of the lifting representations. Overall, our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the lifting representations of finite reductive groups and provide a useful tool for studying their properties.

GeoSim: Realistic Video Simulation via Geometry-Aware Composition for Self-Driving Cars introduces a new approach to video simulation for autonomous vehicles. By leveraging a geometry-aware composition algorithm, GeoSim produces highly realistic simulations that accurately represent the physical environment. The approach takes into account the geometry of the scene, including the location and orientation of objects, to create simulations that closely mimic real-world driving conditions. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of GeoSim's performance and demonstrates its effectiveness in enhancing the training of self-driving cars.

This paper presents a new approach for approximating quantum gates using lattices. We propose a novel method for performing quantum operations on qubits by utilizing the mathematical concept of lattices to approximate the desired quantum gates. Our approach involves the use of a set of quantum gates that are chosen from a set of approximating gates and arranged in a lattice-based model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through the approximation of the Hadamard gate and the CNOT gate. We also discuss some potential applications of our method for the implementation of quantum algorithms and error correction.

This paper introduces WavePacket, a Matlab software package designed for the simulation and analysis of quantum mechanical systems. WavePacket is primarily focused on time-dependent propagation and spectral analysis of closed quantum systems. This first part of the paper covers distinct features of the software such as Discrete Variable Representations (DVR), which permits convenient basis transformations between position and momentum space. Its capabilities include the calculation of dynamics of quantum systems and usage of various types of potentials. Extensive illustrative material - tutorials, demos, videos - complement the package and provide selected applications from molecular quantum dynamics, laser-matter interaction, and quantum optics. The combination of a user-friendly interface, efficient numerical algorithms, and extensive tutorial material makes WavePacket an invaluable tool for both teaching and research in quantum dynamics.

C-Flow: Conditional Generative Flow Models for Images and 3D Point Clouds
Abstract:
In this paper, we propose C-Flow, a novel generative flow model that can generate high-quality images and 3D point clouds conditioned on arbitrary input distributions. C-Flow is based on a conditional generative flow model that learns to map input distributions to output distributions using a sequence of conditionally parameterized transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of C-Flow on image generation tasks, including image inpainting, style transfer, and super-resolution, as well as on 3D point cloud generation tasks, including point cloud completion and point cloud synthesis. Our experiments show that C-Flow outperforms state-of-the-art generative models on these tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets.

> A common problem in medical imaging data analysis is the issue of image segmentation. Segmentation tasks can be carried out using pixel-wise classification where output is generated for each pixel in the image. The output is often a binary mask that allows the user to distinguish between the parts of the image of interest and the background. The segmentation is carried out in different ways using neural networks. However, the major constraint of these neural networks comes from data acquisition. It is not always easy to acquire a data set with a large enough amount of labeled data making the training of deep networks more difficult. In this research work, we explore alternative ways to create segmentation labels from limited manually or automatically labeled data. The approach is based on corrupting the pixel intensities with a random amount and from this new set of values, pixels with intensities in the range that separates the two classes are labeled as positive (object pixels) and the rest of the pixels as background (negative pixels). In this research we show the feasibility of our approach on a liver segmentation task on the CBIS-DDSM dataset. We use a simple U-Net (convolutional neural network that can carry out segmentation task) backbone with three different architectures. Each architecture is followed by a 1D-convolutional layer and we use the mean of the sigmoids of the two outputs of this final layer as segmentation mask for each class. Our results indicate that the performance is better with the U-Net architecture compared to its variants with the proposed meta corrupted pixels (MCP) corruption.

This paper explores the application and significance of background-foreground segmentation technology in the automotive industry, specifically relating to interior sensing. The study introduces an innovative algorithm to improve the effectiveness of in-vehicle sensing systems. The major focus is on successfully separating the foreground (passengers) from the background (interior of the vehicle) in various lighting and occlusion scenarios, thus providing increased monitoring accuracy and ensuring a higher standard of automotive safety. Consequently, the approach facilitates reliable detection and tracking of passengers, contributing to the advancements in the field of self-driving vehicles as well. Results indicate that the proposed model outperforms existing methods in terms of precision and efficiency in real-world testing, thus demonstrating its potential for practical implementation.

This paper presents a novel approach to semantic image segmentation using Convolutional Conditional Random Fields (ConvCRFs). Semantic segmentation, the task of labeling every pixel in an image based on its semantic class, is a key challenge in computer vision due to the significant spatial and contextual intricacies required for high-level understanding of visual data. The proposed ConvCRFs framework leverages the strengths of both Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), utilizing the efficient inference mechanisms of the former and the powerful contextual modeling capability of the latter. Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets demonstrate a consistent improvement in segmentation accuracy over baseline methods, thereby establishing ConvCRFs as a promising tool for semantic image segmentation.

We present a novel method to construct an image representation in the absence of prior knowledge about biological phenomena that needs neither prior experimental evidence nor mathematical formulations (e.g, Bayesian inference). We implement a classification model that takes as input any number of human images and as output a set of points on the image which is related to those visual elements based solely on their semantic relationships with corresponding cells at various scales. The resulting classifier outputs a binary distribution: 1 or 0—i.e., if a row pair occurs together it corresponds to one pixel of membrane segment, else it indicates a different cell. The objective function we implemented has nonlinearity along both sides giving the possibility of finding subclasses for more complex structures like small hair follicles in different tissues. Our system uses only known functions and equations for fitting to our data and requires minimal user training without requiring special skills needed to program, yet produces good results on many image features and neural networks in high dimensional settings. Further, using a single computation cycle we can generate as much as one billion pixel per second of image data using memory bandwidth similar to modern CPUs (in terms of number of cores); this capability will enable us to perform next-generation imaging techniques for advanced health care applications with unprecedented speed with almost no computational overhead.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for capturing omni-range context in order to improve the accuracy and efficiency of omnidirectional image segmentation. Our method leverages a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and spatial pyramid pooling (SPP) to effectively capture both local and global features within an image, enabling accurate segmentation across various scales and orientations.

Existing approaches often struggle with accurately segmenting objects or regions that are partially occluded or have varying sizes and angles, as they rely on fixed-size receptive fields that neglect important contextual information. To address these limitations, our proposed method adopts an SPP module that increases the receptive field size adaptively according to the distance from the center of the feature map, allowing it to capture larger ranges of context while preserving spatial details.

We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. We also conduct thorough ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our method and provide insights into their contributions.

Our main findings show that:

* The integration of SPP with CNNs enhances the representation capability of the network, resulting in improved segmentation performance.
* Adaptive expansion of the receptive field based on distance helps capture both local and global context effectively.
* The use of omni-range context enables better handling of variable object sizes and orientations, leading to improved segmentation accuracy.

The presented method has far-reaching implications for applications that require robust image segmentation, such as autonomous driving, robotics, medical imaging, and video surveillance. Our work contributes to advancing the state-of-the-art in omnidirectional image segmentation and paves the way for more sophisticated applications of computer vision technology.

The paper "On the Compositionality of Quantitative Information Flow" explores the concept of compositionality in the context of quantitative information flow. Compositionality refers to the ability of a system to combine individual components in a way that produces a predictable and meaningful result. In the context of quantitative information flow, this means that the flow of information between different parts of a system can be modeled using mathematical equations that take into account the properties of the individual components.

The paper begins by defining the concept of quantitative information flow and discussing its importance in various fields, including engineering, finance, and computer science. It then goes on to explore the mathematical models that can be used to represent quantitative information flow, including differential equations, partial differential equations, and stochastic processes.

The paper also discusses the concept of compositionality in more detail, and provides examples of how it can be applied to real-world problems. For instance, it shows how compositionality can be used to model the flow of fluids in a pipe, the behavior of financial markets, and the spread of diseases in a population.

Overall, the paper demonstrates that compositionality is a powerful tool for understanding and predicting the behavior of complex systems that involve quantitative information flow. It provides a theoretical framework for modeling such systems and shows how this framework can be applied to a wide range of real-world problems.

This paper presents a novel approach to segmenting scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) images using variational methods and empirical wavelets. STM images are known for their high spatial resolution and ability to capture detailed information about surface topography, but they can be challenging to analyze due to noise and artifacts. In this work, we propose a two-stage approach that first applies a variational method to denoise the image, followed by an empirical wavelet transform to segregate features at different scales.

The variational method used in our approach is based on a total variation (TV) regularization term, which promotes piecewise constant solutions while preserving edges. We solve the resulting optimization problem using a gradient descent algorithm, and demonstrate its effectiveness in removing noise while retaining important details in the image.

Next, we apply an empirical wavelet transform to the denoised image, using a set of basis functions with different scales and orientations. The wavelet coefficients are then thresholded to separate signal from noise, and the resulting binary mask is used to segment the image into regions of interest. We show that this approach effectively identifies features such as atomic steps, terraces, and vacancies, and provides improved performance compared to traditional thresholding techniques.

Our proposed method offers several advantages over existing approaches to STM image segmentation. Firstly, it does not require any prior knowledge about the location or orientation of features in the image. Secondly, it uses a non-parametric technique to model the noise distribution, making it more robust than methods relying on Gaussian assumptions. Finally, the use of empirical wavelets allows us to adapt to the multiscale nature of STM images, leading to better feature detection and separation.

We validate our approach using a dataset of STM images captured under different conditions, and compare the results to those obtained using other state-of-the-art methods. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.

Overall, this paper makes an important contribution to the field of STM image analysis by introducing a powerful new tool for extracting meaningful information from noisy and complex data

This study investigates the universality of two fundamental relations in galaxy evolution: the luminosity-metallicity (LZ) relation and the mass-metallicity (MZ) relation, specifically for compact star-forming galaxies within the redshift range of 0 to 3. By analyzing a large sample of these galaxies with various observational data sets, we aim to determine if these relationships remain consistent across cosmic time or if they evolve differently based on environment/structure changes during different epochs. Our findings suggest that while there is some scatter in the LZ and MZ relations throughout this period, their overall shape remains relatively constant indicating a universal behavior among compact star-forming galaxies regardless of redshift. This suggests that processes governing chemical enrichment and stellar population synthesis play important roles in shaping these systems over vast stretches of cosmological time.

> An emerging topic in video analysis is temporal alignment of content based video representation over time. To facilitate it, we present a video annotation system for object regions in each frame in a video. These object regions are automatically extracted with a graph cut segmentation algorithm. The segmentation result is then analyzed carefully to determine the pixel level object labels. These labels are further organized to provide temporal annotation over video in form of semantic segmentation. The proposed segmentation approach is based on both spatial and temporal information of the input video sequence. Since the semantic annotation is often performed with a labeling algorithm that operates over pixels, the accuracy of the label is quite sensitive to the quality of the input video image. As a result poor quality images can lead to erroneous labeling. We therefore developed a new distortion-aware video segmentation and labeling technique based on spatially adaptive feature extraction techniques for reliable video semantic segmentation across various distortion conditions. Our proposed distortion-aware labeling method outperforms the state of the art baseline labeling method.

> Building a quantum network connecting multiple sites is a promising route toward quantum internet. The major building blocks of a quantum network are quantum links that provide two-way quantum communication and node devices, which include quantum data storage and processing. In this manuscript, we propose a recursive network construction method based on the superposition principle enabled by the reversible quantum logic gates. Using this scheme, we implement a recursive quantum repeater network and realize an arbitrary connectivity between the involved nodes. We analyze the recursion depth of the repeater network to obtain the optimal and minimum node number required for constructing the quantum connectivity. We also show the feasibility and the scalability of the proposed repeater network with the current experimental technology. Our quantum repeater network scheme can be realized in existing ion trap quantum computer systems while allowing the quantum communication between remote ions.

In this paper, we present the WavePacket package, a MATLAB toolbox for numerical simulation of quantum dynamics. The package is designed to provide an efficient and user-friendly platform for studying the behavior of quantum systems, with a focus on closed systems and discrete variable representations.

WavePacket provides a comprehensive set of tools for generating and manipulating wave packets, computing expectation values, and visualizing quantum dynamics. It supports a variety of quantum systems, including spin chains, oscillators, and two-level systems, and allows for the simulation of both time-dependent and time-independent Hamiltonians.

The package includes a range of algorithms for solving the time-dependent and time-independent Schrödinger equations, including the finite difference, finite element, and pseudospectral methods. It also provides a variety of pre-defined wave functions and operators, as well as tools for creating custom wave functions and observables.

WavePacket is designed to be user-friendly, with a focus on ease of use and intuitive syntax. It includes a comprehensive documentation and a set of tutorial examples to help users get started quickly.

Overall, WavePacket is a powerful tool for studying quantum dynamics, and it has the potential to be a valuable resource for researchers and educators in the field of quantum physics.

This paper presents a new measure of economic complexity, based on the idea that economies with higher levels of productivity and innovation tend to have more complex structures. The proposed measure is derived from a simple model of production in which firms can choose their level of specialization and efficiency. We show how this choice affects the overall structure of the economy, leading to a natural definition of economic complexity as the degree of specialization across industries. Our measure has several desirable properties: it is easy to compute using standard data on industry-level productivity; it captures both within-industry and between-industry complexity; and it provides a useful benchmark for comparing countries or regions at different stages of development. We illustrate our approach with examples from several developed and developing countries, showing that our measure successfully captures differences in economic complexity across regions and time periods.

The Multi-Compound Transformer is a novel approach for accurate biomedical image segmentation. It utilizes a combination of transformer-based models and compound segmentation to achieve state-of-the-art results. Medical image segmentation is a critical task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from diagnosis to treatment planning. However, the performance of segmentation models can be limited by the availability of labeled training data, which is often scarce and expensive to obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to knowledge transfer for medical image segmentation that is network-agnostic, meaning it can be applied to any deep learning-based segmentation model. Our approach involves leveraging a pre-trained model on a large dataset to transfer knowledge to a target model on a smaller dataset, without requiring any additional labeled data. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation performance compared to state-of-the-art methods that do not utilize knowledge transfer. Our results suggest that knowledge transfer is a powerful technique for improving the performance of medical image segmentation models, and that our approach can be easily applied to a wide range of segmentation models and datasets.

We describe a novel approach to efficient interactive image segmentation. Our technique takes the best from two worlds. On the one hand, we harness the capabilities of deep learning to generate image features and perform pixel classification. On the other hand, we exploit classical graphics optimization and rendering techniques to efficiently explore solution space and speed up interactive selection process.

Our solution consists of two components. The first is an efficient interactive technique that relies on graphics hardware to perform fast segmentation refinement. We use the method of level sets to perform fast image editing, making use of multiple graphics hardware back-ends and relying on asynchronous workloads to provide an efficient runtime.The second component is a novel convolutional neural network for semantic segmentation, which integrates both pixel intensity and edge map as input. The network takes as input color and edge information of all images in a dataset and outputs a joint edge map and segmentation. We use the segmentation results and the edge map to update and refine our interactive segmentation process.

We evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of our technique by performing automatic and interactive segmentation on multiple datasets, including fine grained (BSDS500) and medical (NIH and BRATS) problems. Experimental results demonstrate good object tracking performance, improved accuracy when compared to state of the art techniques with respect to intersection over union when used as the segmentation backend for level set optimization, and efficiency when performed interactively.

More technical details, results and comparisons are provided in the full version of this paper.

Accurate biomedical image segmentation is crucial for diagnosis and treatment of various diseases. Deep learning techniques have shown promising results in this field, but still face challenges in handling complex images with diverse structures and low contrast. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning architecture called FANet (Feedback Attention Network), which incorporates feedback attention mechanisms to improve the segmentation accuracy.

The proposed FANet consists of two main components: a feedforward network and a feedback network. The feedforward network extracts features from the input image using convolutional layers, while the feedback network refines the feature representations by iteratively attending to the most relevant regions. The feedback attention mechanism allows the network to focus on the areas that are difficult to segment, enhancing the performance of the model.

We evaluate the effectiveness of FANet using several publicly available datasets, including brain tumor segmentation, liver segmentation, and lung nodule detection. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation models, achieving an average dice similarity coefficient of 0.83, 0.91, and 0.87 for brain tumor, liver, and lung nodule segmentation, respectively.

In addition, we conduct extensive ablation studies to analyze the contributions of different components in FANet. The results show that the feedback attention module significantly improves the segmentation accuracy, especially when dealing with complex images. Furthermore, we visualize the attention maps generated by FANet, providing insights into how the network allocates attention to different parts of the input image.

Our work has important implications for biomedical image segmentation tasks, as it demonstrates the potential of feedback attention networks in improving segmentation accuracy and robustness. Future research can build upon these findings to further enhance the performance of FANet and explore its applications in other medical imaging modalities.

Abstract: Medical image segmentation plays a pivotal role in aiding physicians with diagnosis and treatment. Compared to other modalities, the curability of lung CT images poses a unique challenge. In this paper, we aim to provide an in-depth analysis of popular evaluation metrics, with a focus on dice score and Jaccard index, for medical image segmentation. We analyze the sensitivity of these metrics to different types of errors and discuss the implications on algorithm design. We propose an optimized Dice score and Jaccard index evaluation framework, with a focus on CT images, which integrates a collection of improvements targeting lung CT images. This framework is publicly available as the DICEJaccard package. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on the public LLIDE dataset. Our framework achieves ≈85% speedup with ≈88% memory reduction. We show through experiments the advantage of our framework over the commonly used Eval studiomatch framework and other alternative implementations. We further discuss potential ways to effectively use these metrics for automatic lung segmentation evaluation.

In the field of machine learning, training models on data from a single source often leads to suboptimal performance on data from other sources. This is especially true when the data from different sources are not directly comparable, such as images from different cameras. To address this issue, domain adaptation methods aim to adapt models trained on one source to another. However, most existing domain adaptation methods require a large amount of data from both the source and target domains, which may not be available in many practical applications. In this paper, we proposed mDALU, a novel multi-source domain adaptation and label unification framework that can handle partial datasets. mDALU consists of two main components: (1) a domain adaptation module that adapts models trained on multiple source domains to a target domain, and (2) a label unification module that unifies the labels of the data from multiple source domains. We evaluated the performance of mDALU on two benchmark datasets: Office-31 and Office-Home. The results showed that mDALU outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both datasets.

This paper presents a novel approach for semantics-aware multi-modal domain translation, specifically from LiDAR point clouds to panoramic color images. The proposed method leverages the semantic information present in the LiDAR point clouds to generate more accurate and visually appealing panoramic color images. The authors introduce a new network architecture that combines a semantic segmentation network with a generative adversarial network to perform the translation. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in generating high-quality panoramic color images that preserve the semantic information from the LiDAR point clouds. The proposed method has potential applications in various domains such as autonomous driving and virtual reality.

This paper presents a Bayesian Dense Inverse Searching (BDIS) algorithm designed for real-time stereo matching in minimally invasive surgery. The primary objective of the proposed algorithm is to accurately determine the depth information from 2D stereo endoscope images, essential for assisting surgeons during operative procedures. The BDIS algorithm leverages the Bayesian framework, thus ensuring a probabilistically sound stereo correspondence. It also incorporates an inverse searching strategy to enhance the search efficiency, facilitating real-time application. The effectiveness of the algorithm was rigorously tested on public datasets and live surgeries, demonstrating increased accuracy and speed over existing solutions. This development is of paramount importance to the field of computer-assisted surgery, promising to improve surgical precision, reduce operational risk, and consequently, enhance patient safety.

"We propose a novel technique for estimating the fraction of patients correctly assigned as having a heart attack based on a single photograph of the subject taken over their lifetime, under controlled monitoring conditions. We provide numerical and numerical simulations of three different techniques for image segmentation, namely, an MNI-based approach based on a linear transformation of the subject's face, a cross-platform implementation with C++ based code-generation and a hybrid approach with a neural network. The first approach, which optimally estimates the fraction of patients correctly assigned as having a heart attack on a standard set of faces, achieves an accuracy of 0.6%. However, when faced with a significantly more complex set of faces, the method fails to achieve a sufficiently good result as to be practical for real clinical applications. This failure occurs because of the inherent variation in the quality of the training images themselves. Using cross-platform image segmentation with C++ and our algorithms achieves about a 90% confidence level, a level better than those obtained with our simpler method. At a more stringent 95% confidence level, the best results are achieved with our hybrid approach. We show that the latter approach is a promising replacement for our less efficient but more accurate method."

Nernst's postulate is one of the fundamental principles in theoretical physics which connects classical and quantum mechanics. In this work, we consider a Casimir system consisting of two parallel conducting plates separated by a small distance, and study the relationship between Nernst Theorem and Casimir-Lifshitz free energy at finite temperatures. The first step is to evaluate the vacuum thermal conductivity on the surface of each plate based on the Casimir effect induced in these surfaces due to the presence of other plate. Then using the first law of thermodynamics, we derive an expression for the total Casimir-lifshitz free energy as function of temperature of each plate and their separation. Finally, we verify that our obtained results satisfy Nernst Theorem constraints on electron flux, and energy in terms of electric current. We show that our study generalizes the previous works by taking into consideration also the energy density of the vacuum state resulting from quantum fluctuations which provides the correct interpretation of Nernst Theorem in the context of Casimir systems at finite temperature.

The decidability of various types of coded messages including multiset code, set code, and numerally encrypted figure cryptogram is examined. The author provides a comprehensive analysis of each type of cipher, discussing their historical context as well as modern applications. Through this examination, the author concludes that while some forms of these ciphers are undecidable, others can be solved with relative ease using methods such as frequency analysis or brute force tactics. In this paper, we propose a new end-to-end trainable deep active contour model for automated image segmentation, with the aim of delineating buildings in aerial imagery. The proposed model is based on a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) that is trained to directly output the desired segmentation results. The CNN is then used as an initialization for a traditional active contour model, which is fine-tuned using a simple gradient descent algorithm. The entire system is end-to-end trainable, and can be optimized using standard backpropagation. We evaluate the proposed model on a publicly available dataset of aerial images, and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods for building segmentation.

We introduce PC-U, an algorithm that enables high-quality reconstruction and segmentation, both spatially and temporally, of cardiac walls using CT imaging data. Our procedure achieves these effects by: (i) first constructing and then applying a multiplanar algorithm to an accurate 3D reconstruction of a complex region of interest ('W'); or alternatively in a constrained 2D framework; (ii) taking advantage of the information learned within W, such as the direction and position of all wall surfaces; (iii) estimating the surface geometry parameters independently at subregions at each side angle. We demonstrate its applicability to both single and multiple subjects using real heart muscle scans taken with the NICE II system at Stanford University Hospital. This study includes the application of the tool on five patients' cardiac walls at two different levels of CT quality (100 μg/s with low signal intensity, and 500 Hz with good signal). The technique yields a high level of detailed information about each patient's wall geometry. We validate PC-U performance on one case study and report its overall results across three cases and four patients.

This paper presents an innovative approach to semantic segmentation in pathology using an Adaptive Weighting Multi-Field-of-View Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The study aims to address the challenges of varying sizes and shapes of regions of interest in pathological images. The proposed model integrates multiple fields of view in a single network, allowing it to adaptively learn and weight different scales of context. The model's performance was evaluated on two public histopathological datasets, demonstrating superior results compared to existing methods. This research contributes to the advancement of automated pathological image analysis, potentially improving diagnostic accuracy and efficiency.

In this paper, we explore extensions of Lie algebras of differential operators and their applications in various areas of mathematics and physics. We begin by discussing the basic concepts and properties of Lie algebras of differential operators, including their definition, representation theory, and relationship to symmetries of differential equations.

Next, we examine different types of extensions of Lie algebras of differential operators, such as central extensions, conformal extensions, and pseudo-central extensions. We also discuss the cohomology of these extensions and its role in understanding their structure and properties.

One of the main focuses of the paper is on the application of extended Lie algebras of differential operators in mathematical physics, particularly in the study of integrable systems and quantum field theories. We show how certain extensions can be used to generate new conservation laws and symmetries, leading to novel insights into the behavior of physical systems.

The paper also touches upon the connection between extension deformations of Lie algebras of differential operators and deformations of algebraic structures, such as associative algebras and nonassociative algebras. This allows us to view extensions of Lie algebras of differential operators as part of a larger framework of deformation theory.

Finally, we discuss open problems and future directions in the field of extended Lie algebras of differential operators, highlighting potential research directions and applications in both mathematics and physics.

Overall, our work provides a comprehensive overview of extensions of Lie algebras of differential operators, shedding light on their rich structure and diverse applications. It will serve as a valuable resource for mathematicians and physicists interested in the interplay between Lie theory, differential geometry, and mathematical physics.

We propose a novel technique to hierarchically partition n-dimensional space into a collection of super-regions, each of which is locally flat. Our approach is based on a hierarchical clustering of region boundaries, which are approximated by a constant function. The resulting piecewise-constant super-regions can be thought of as a generalization of Voronoi cells, where the Voronoi diagram is replaced by a more general clustering structure. We show that our technique can be used to efficiently compute hierarchy-preserving super-regions, which can be used to approximate n-dimensional functions with a smaller number of parameters. We also show that our technique can be used to improve the performance of existing algorithms for computing Voronoi diagrams and Delaunay triangulations.

The novel explores themes of love, culture, and identity, and ultimately asks questions about the nature of relationships and the impact of cultural differences on personal connections.

> We introduce a new class of deformations of Hopf algebras, called additive deformations. These deformations are defined by a family of additive maps on the underlying vector space of the Hopf algebra. We show that the class of additive deformations is closed under the usual operations of deformation theory, such as the tensor product and the convolution product. We also show that the class of additive deformations is closed under the operation of taking the dual Hopf algebra. We give a number of examples of additive deformations, including the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_n)$. We also show that the class of additive deformations is closed under the operation of taking the dual Hopf algebra.

In this paper, we introduce RatLesNetv2, an image segmentation system for rodent brains for use in the field of systems neurobiology. Previous models for the segmentation of microscopy images of rodent brain slices have required thousands of segmentations to train, and have suffered from a trade-off between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency.

RatLesNetv2 is based on the original architecture of U-Net [32], a deep feed-forward network. The network architecture is composed of encoding and decoding phases to extract deep semantic information from the input image and up-sample it back to the original resolution, respectively. Encoding is accomplished with two parallel convolutional paths, where each starts with a convolutional block with multiple convolutional layers and produces a feature map with double size. The decoding path follows the same structure up-sampling the feature map back to the original size of the input image, while skipping connections merge features in the lower resolution path.
We trained RatLesNetv2 on 1400 images for 4 different label classes. A leave-one-out cross validation scheme was used to test the model performance. The model provides a high performance trade-off between computation time and accuracy (~15 minutes per image on 4 high-end NVIDIA GTX 1080 GPUs), and provides consistent performance across all lesion types on different brain slices. The complete code is available for free, under the MIT Open-source license through GitHub (link in the paper).

In this work, we demonstrate joint processing of medical image features such as brightness, rotation, color, etc., in a manner that resembles standard approaches to face recognition and object localization and thus provide an efficient and tractable basis for future work on training image-guided methods. The state-of-the-art state-of-the art methods do not explicitly embed feature representations such as features into the networks; instead they use linear activation function (LF) schemes, which lead to significant overfitting as described by [Caklinas et al., 2011]. In contrast, our system utilizes three basic feature structures directly learned directly from human perception, i.e., luminance, rotation, color, sharpness, etc., and embeds them in the neural network itself. These constructions are then embedded into the underlying convolutional neural network as unsupervised feature extractors. It results in highly flexible, highly useful CNN based models with few assumptions and very little generalization requirements beyond what could be applied to previously trained CNNs—resulting in rapid adoption by many healthcare applications and even by vision systems.

Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in the United States, affecting more than 2.7 million people. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is an effective treatment for AFib; however, approximately 20% of patients experience postoperative recurrence. It is critical to identify patients at high risk of recurrence after RFA for targeted medical therapy. This study proposes a deep learning-based approach to estimate postoperative AFib recurrence using standard 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs).

A total of 167 patients who underwent RFA for symptomatic drug-refractory AFib between August 2016 and July 2020 were included in this study. For each patient, the standard 12-lead ECG recorded on the first postoperative day was used for model training and validation. Two deep learning models were developed and compared: a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a attention-based deep neural network (DNN). The models were trained to classify ECGs into either with or without AFib recurrence. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) was used to compare the performance of the two models.

The results showed that the CNN model had an AUC-ROC of 0.80, while the DNN model had an AUC-ROC of 0.85. The DNN model performed better than the CNN model in estimating postoperative AFib recurrence. The DNN model may be a useful tool for estimating the risk of AFib recurrence in patients who have undergone RFA.

This study demonstrates the potential of deep learning in estimating postoperative AFib recurrence using standard 12-lead ECGs. This approach may help identify patients at high risk of recurrence and guide targeted medical therapy.

In this paper, we explore the relationship between toric Kähler metrics and compact tropical amoebas. We first introduce the concept of toric Kähler metrics and their connection to moment angle maps. We then discuss the idea of viewing these metrics from infinity, which allows us to establish a link with quantized algebraic geometry.

Using this perspective, we show that compact tropical amoebas can be used to study the geometry of toric Kähler manifolds. In particular, we demonstrate that the metric properties of the toric Kähler manifold are reflected in the tropical amoeba, providing a new tool for studying these spaces.

Our results have applications in both mathematics and physics, as they provide a novel way of understanding the relationship between algebraic and symplectic geometry on one hand, and quantum field theory and string theory on the other. The techniques developed here also open up new directions for research into the geometry and Topology of toric varieties and orbifolds.

Overall, our work provides original insights into the structure and behavior of toric Kähler manifolds and compact tropical amoebas, offering fresh perspectives and techniques for studying these fascinating objects.

The aim of our work is to improve the performance of object proposal generation in various computer vision tasks such as instance segmentation and object detection. We propose an algorithm that combines submodular optimization with deep learning principles to selectively focus on regions containing specific objects or characteristics within an image. Augmented reality (AR) applications have recently received considerable attention for their potential benefits in medical image analysis. However, most AR research has focused on 2D image data, while 3D data, which provides more informative visual cues, remains under-explored. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap by developing a framework for 3D medical image segmentation with weakly-supervised learning and user-friendly collaborative training. We introduce a new weakly-supervised loss function based on an adversarial objective and combine it with a collaborative training strategy. The proposed method enables users with limited expertise to contribute to the training process and improve segmentation performance. Furthermore, we propose a latent space data augmentation technique that can generate new training samples from existing ones, which is essential for training deep neural networks with limited data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three different 3D medical image segmentation tasks using brain MRI, abdominal CT, and cardiac CT scans. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the public BraTS 2020 segmentation benchmark with a weakly-supervised approach.

This paper presents a novel Transformation Consistent Self-ensembling Model (TCSM) for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. We propose a new approach to improve the effectiveness and reliability of semi-supervised learning by exploiting unlabeled data in an ensemble fashion. Our TCSM employs a transformation consistency loss function, which maintains the prediction consistency between original and transformed images. The model also introduces a self-ensembling mechanism that averages the model’s weights over training iterations, reducing the risk of overfitting and enhancing stability. Comparative evaluation on two public medical imaging datasets, ISIC 2018 and LiTS 2017, demonstrates our model's superior performance over state-of-the-art methods in terms of intersection over union (IoU) and dice coefficient (DC). This research underlines the potential of semi-supervised learning approaches for efficient medical image analysis, especially when dealing with limited labeled data.

These projections preserve relevant information from the original distribution while reducing computational complexity. In “Transform a Set”, we follow a data-driven approach to jointly reason about the generation of image collages and their layout. We tackle the problem as an image retrieval and transformation task, where image collages are generated from a given set of images by applying specified transformations. This paper examines the application of function norms to deep networks, demonstrating their effectiveness as a regularization technique. We introduce a novel method of applying function norms to deep networks, which we call "function regularization." This method involves optimizing the function norms of the weights and biases in the network, in addition to the usual optimization of the network's loss function.

We show that function regularization can improve the generalization performance of deep networks, leading to better performance on a variety of tasks. We also show that function regularization can help reduce overfitting and improve the stability of the training process.

This paper discusses the theoretical properties of function norms and their application to deep networks. We also present experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of function regularization on a variety of deep learning tasks, including image classification, object detection, and natural language processing.

Overall, this paper presents a novel and effective method of regularizing deep networks, which has the potential to improve the performance and robustness of deep learning systems.

An autonomous vehicle is one that can sense its environment and operate without human involvement. Computer stereo vision is an important component of autonomous vehicles, as it allows the vehicle to perceive and understand its surroundings in three dimensions. This paper discusses the challenges and opportunities of computer stereo vision for autonomous driving, including methods for accurate obstacle detection and distance estimation. Additionally, this paper explores the potential of computer stereo vision for scene understanding and behavior prediction in complex environments. The proposed methods are evaluated through extensive experimental validation, demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed approaches.

In this paper, we propose improved control strategies for intermittent contact mode atomic force microscopes. We address the challenge of maintaining stable imaging and data acquisition while minimizing damage to the sample surface caused by continuous tapping. Our approach involves a combination of adaptive feedback algorithms, real-time analysis of cantilever deflection signals, and optimization techniques that enable seamless transitions between controlled indentation and retraction modes. Through both simulation studies and experimental validation on various samples, including biological macromolecules and soft materials, our methodology demonstrates enhanced image quality, faster scanning rates, and reduced usage of the piezo scanner, thus offering an efficient alternative to conventional AC modulation schemes in AFM operation.

Arrival of patients at the emergency department (ED) with unclear diagnosis poses a great challenge to clinicians due to the time-critical nature of the decisions involved. In this paper, we present MCU-Net, a deep learning framework for assisting with the referral of patients with unclear diagnoses from the ED to the appropriate specialty departments. More specifically, given the initial symptoms of a patient, MCU-Net outputs a referral recommendation along with the uncertainty of the recommendation. The referral recommendations and uncertainties are synthesized into a novel visualization, which augments the referring clinician's decision process. We demonstrate through a qualitative study that our framework has the potential to become a decision support tool for clinicians, helping them to make more informed referral decisions.

"We present a method for detecting curves in depth maps for cultural heritage object exploration. The proposed method uses a machine learning-based approach to determine whether a certain pixel with a specific depth value belongs to a curve-structure or is not part of that structure. A key objective of this paper is to determine the depth of the curve-structure and its orientation from a single depth map without requiring other auxiliary data, e.g., 3D models or texture images. A CNN-based (Convolutional Neural Networks) approach is presented, which takes as its input a patch of pixels in a depth map, followed by a convolutional layer to learn the relation for the specific scene. The method is generic in the sense that it does not require any pre-training with curve-structures for a specific object. The trained model is generic in the sense that it can be applied to depth maps without requiring any other objects. It can detect a curve at various depth values and estimate the 3D position of a line-curve (a planar curve). In comparison with prior art, the proposed method detects curves even if the image plane is occluded and the surface of the object can be curved. The proposed approach is evaluated on real world datasets. Furthermore, the approach is used to interact with heritage objects by extracting the curve structure for 2D interaction of users on touch screens with virtual copies of the heritage object. The results show the usefulness of the proposed approach for 2D virtual object interactions in heritage and museum exhibitions and applications."

The story follows the life of Alex, a struggling writer who dreams of being successful. Every night before going to sleep, he lights candles all around his apartment and imagines himself living in a lavish mansion with his books lining every shelf. However, when he wakes up, his room always looks untouched, leaving him wondering if it's all just a dream.

One day, while lighting up the candles, an old woman across the hall confronted him about her fear that the candles were too close to the curtains. She turned out to be his estranged grandmother who had abandoned him as a child, but now needed help due to illness. Alex realized she was trying to get through to him after years apart, so he decided to help take care of her until her passing.

Meanwhile, he continued working on his writing, participating regularly in local poetry contests hoping to finally gain recognition for his talents. With his newfound sense of purpose and the support from family, he began making small progresses, winning minor awards for his poems.

As time went by, Alex’s connection to his grandmother deepened, and he used her advice, stories, and even some of words she spoke to infuse more depth into his characters and themes. His poetic work was becoming more powerful and relatable, but with grander ambitions came greater challenges.

During one visit to the hospital, Alex discovered his grandmother had fallen ill again – this time, critically. He rushed to make amends with their past issues, vowing to protect her throughout whatever happened next. During a final meeting at her bedside, they discussed future goals, regrets, and memories shared during her long journey. In the end, she encouraged Alex to find happiness in what he does best: sharing his passions through his art.

With grief heavy but resolve strong, Alex returned home determined to follow in his grandmother's footsteps and achieve success while keeping her memory alive.

In Emily Climbs, our protagonist is an introverted young woman named Emily who has always been terrified of heights but decides to confront her fear by climbing Mount Kilimanjaro with her extroverted best friend Rose. Along their journey up the mountain and through various challenges such as harsh weather conditions and physical strain, we see both characters grow and change as they bond over shared experiences and push themselves beyond what they thought was possible. Through this adventure, Emily learns to trust in herself and conquer her fears while also discovering that life isn't just about taking risks; it's about embracing new opportunities and finding inner strength from within.

We present an automatic color image segmentation method based on a square elemental region-based seeding and merging method, which can be used to automatically extract color information from images with low spatial resolution. The algorithm uses a simple geometric model that allows us to efficiently compute the color values in a given pixel area. We demonstrate our approach by extracting color information from a set of images taken at different resolutions (640×480 pixels) using only a few hundred lines of code. Our results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and speed.
