*"Many MOOCs strive to have large participation rates for each online
  course in order to attract more students. However, research has found
  that the participation rate generally decreases rapidly over the course
  period, regardless of the instructor, content, or platform. A
  possible explanation for this decline is that the information
  exchange among students is not sufficient to maintain their interest.
  
  The information exchange in most MOOCs (or other crowdsourced
  learning environments) happens either through a forum platform or
  through Q&A websites. However, previous studies found that the
  information exchanged through forums and Q&A websites is limited and
  unrepresentative. The limited information exchange may not be
  conducive to students' learning. In this paper, we conduct the first
  extensive empirical study to systematically investigate the communication
  patterns among the students in MOOCs. Our experimental results suggest
  that only the students who were enrolled for the same module, the
  same problem set, the same lecture, or the same homework assignment
  have the similar learning difficulties and therefore the similar
  communication needs. Thus, the information exchange in MOOCs is very
  limited and communication between students who do not have the similar
  problems often fails to happen. Based on the findings, we analyze the
  shortcomings in current crowdsourced platforms and propose some novel
  mechanisms that can be incorporated into the platform to facilitate
  the information exchange among students with different learning
  needs.

In this paper, we propose a new method for context-based segmentation from weak labels using adversarial networks. Our method is based on the observation that the context around an object can provide valuable information for its segmentation. To exploit this observation, we first generate object proposals using a region proposal network. We then segment the object proposals using a segmentation network trained with weak labels. Finally, we use an adversarial network to improve the segmentation results by learning the context around the object proposals. Our method is able to segment objects from weakly labeled data with better accuracy than the state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we present a new depth image segmentation method based on histogram of depth. Our method first extracts depth information from a depth image and then segments the image into foreground and background using the histogram of depth. We also show how our method can be used for driver distraction detection. Our method is able to segment depth images in real-time and is scalable to large depth images.

The authors propose a new class of artificial neural networks (ANNs) based on a newly discovered type of recurrent network algorithm called L2-regularized gradient descent (L2GDR) which is commonly used for object detection. L2GDR is based on a relatively new optimization concept known as Generalized and Scalable L-regularized Gradient Descent (Gen-LaneNet), which we propose here by systematically investigating the implementation and use of such algorithms for 3D lane detection in real-time games. Experiments were run using the freely available Unity3D engine to compare Gen-LaneNet to a standard L2GDR implementation and to the previous state-of-the-art for lane detection known as L2GDR+ for video games. Our primary goal was to compare the speed, accuracy and quality of Gen-LaneNet for both visual and non-visual use.

We propose a method for semantic segmentation that combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and conditional random fields (CRFs). Our method, called "convolutional CRFs" (CCRFs), models the output of a CNN as a CRF, where the CRF potentials are defined using a convolutional kernel. This approach allows us to directly model the relationship between pixels in an image, without the need for expensive post-processing steps such as non-maximum suppression. We evaluate our method on the PASCAL VOC 2012 semantic segmentation challenge, and obtain state-of-the-art results.

> Fully automated segmentation of every pixel in an image remains a hard problem. We discuss here a new methodology that gives a fully class-independent solution to this problem. Instead of segmenting the image in one “step”, we divide the task into a number of smaller sequenced steps. Our method relies on the use of a convolutional neural net (CNN) to perform two successive tasks within each step. First, the CNN locates an attention region in the image. This region corresponds potentially to a new object to be classified. Secondly, the CNN identifies any pixel (if one exists) located within this attention region that is the focus of this new classification. Within the sequential frame work, we can then perform the (standard) classification operation on each pixel within this attention region and, using the pointer pixel found by the CNN, predict whether the rest of the attention region will be of the same type or not. The method is class independent as no knowledge of the set of objects to be identified needs to be given during training. We show that the overall performance (segmentation) of the sequential CNN is superior to that of a CNN directly trained to identify new objects and their location in each instance of the image.

Unsupervised feature learning in deep networks has become particularly important these days as it can be used for an infinite range of tasks, such as object detection, classification, translation, speech recognition, translation to foreign languages and so on. However, many challenges still exist with supervised learning: Unveiling hidden structure that may not be revealed by data-correlation techniques (e.g., classification); overfitting; nonlocal interactions leading to excessive nonlinearities or other unanticipated consequences; etc. These problems are more difficult when trained using network architecture not yet fully adapted. The ability to extract hierarchical representations from unmodeled features of complex scenes could provide a way out of this current state because it would let network architectures learn very specific representations by themselves without using examples. We present a new algorithm called TransformNet which incorporates convolutions into its architecture and is based on a bimodal biphasic neuron network model for neural networks that we obtained through joint work with Ting Zhang at University College London. In contrast to simple convolutions, our biphasic convolution produces a biquadratic kernel at each node and the resulting kernels encode three dimensions: depth first, then width and then height. Our aim was to produce a deep convolution layer (conv1d) whose output features were dimensionally similar to those found in any three dimensional image dataset (image2vec), despite being only five layers deep. Using our algorithm, a number of scenes are deconvolved into their respective images. Moreover, the quality results have shown significant improvements over previous attempts. At this point, our goal is to further develop a convolutional and denoising filter which can detect very small objects including human faces within two and even three dimensions, which makes the architecture even deeper and more accurate than ever before!

In medical image segmentation, each pixel is typically associated with a single class label. However, recent studies have shown that considering multiple labels can improve the segmentation accuracy. In this paper, we present a deep supervision framework for multi-label medical image segmentation. Our framework is based on a simple observation: each label represents a unique path from the image to the corresponding output. Therefore, the supervision signals from all the labels can be integrated by considering all the paths from the image to the output. We show that our framework can be applied to two popular deep segmentation networks, U-Net and SegNet, and significantly improve their segmentation accuracy on two medical image segmentation benchmarks: the BraTS 2018 dataset and the ISIC2018 dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/wsk1103/Multi-label-Deep-Supervision.

In the dusty, sun-baked town of Willow Creek, a young girl named Lily grows up on a ranch with her mother, older brother, and grandfather. Lily's mother, a fierce and determined woman, has always struggled to make ends meet, working tirelessly to keep their small ranch afloat despite the challenges of living in a drought-ridden valley. Lily's grandfather, a grizzled old rancher, has seen his share of hardships and has a deep well of wisdom and experience to draw from.

As Lily grows older, she becomes increasingly restless, feeling trapped by the limited opportunities and resources available to her in Willow Creek. She dreams of leaving the valley and making a name for herself in the world beyond, but her mother's determination to keep the ranch running and her grandfather's stubborn refusal to adapt to changing times make it difficult for her to pursue her dreams.

One day, a chance encounter with a group of wild horses changes everything. Lily is drawn to their beauty and freedom, and she becomes determined to tame them and make them her own. With the help of her grandfather and a local horse trainer, Lily sets out to train the wild horses and turn them into a successful horse-riding business.

As Lily works to tame the horses, she learns valuable lessons about perseverance, hard work, and the power of never giving up on her dreams. But as the drought continues to ravage the valley and the ranch struggles to stay afloat, Lily must confront the harsh realities of living in a difficult and unforgiving environment.

Deep learning systems, both in data centers and edge devices, require many hyper-parameters to be carefully tuned to achieve optimum performance. Hyper-parameters such as the learning rate, dropout probability, and number of layers and hidden units heavily influence the performance of the deep learning model. In this paper, we focus on one key hyper-parameter — the number of hidden units — and present a new distributed learning method that estimates this parameter from data in a node-specific manner. We show that our proposed method, which is based on a distributed diffusion-based limited memory (DBLMM) optimization algorithm, can efficiently estimate the optimal number of hidden units on different nodes, even in the presence of hyper-parameters that have undesirable or unhelpful values for otherwise standard optimization algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both synthetic data and also CIFAR-10 data on AWS EC2 instances, where we show that our method can efficiently estimate the number of hidden units, specific to different nodes, that are close to the minimum as judged by the validation error.

> We propose a novel approach to adversarial learning that is based on the idea of learning discriminators as energy networks. The energy network is a neural network that is trained to predict the energy of a given input. The energy of an input is defined as the negative log-likelihood of the input under a given distribution. In our approach, the generator is trained to produce samples that have low energy, while the discriminator is trained to produce samples that have high energy. We show that our approach is able to learn discriminators that are more robust to adversarial attacks than discriminators trained using traditional methods. We also show that our approach is able to learn discriminators that are more accurate than discriminators trained using traditional methods.

The GraphBLAS (Graph-Based Linear Algebra System) is a software library designed to provide efficient and flexible linear algebra operations on graph-structured data. While the practical applications of GraphBLAS have been well-explored in various domains, its mathematical foundations have not been thoroughly examined. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of the mathematical underpinnings of GraphBLAS.

We begin by discussing the motivation behind GraphBLAS and how it differs from traditional linear algebra systems. We then introduce the basic concepts and data structures used in GraphBLAS, including graphs, matrices, and vectors. Next, we present a detailed exposition of the mathematical properties of GraphBLAS's core operations, such as matrix-vector multiplication, sparse matrix representation, and eigenvalue decomposition.

The heart of our analysis lies in establishing the mathematical correctness and efficiency of GraphBLAS's algorithms. We prove that the matrix-vector multiplication operation in GraphBLAS preserves the linearity and spectral properties of the underlying graph, and that the sparse matrix representation adopted by GraphBLAS leads to significant computational savings without sacrificing accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the eigenvalue decomposition algorithm in GraphBLAS is equivalent to the classic Power iteration method, while offering improved scalability and robustness.

Our study also explores the connections between GraphBLAS and other algebraic frameworks, such as graph theory, linear algebra, and machine learning. We show that GraphBLAS can be seen as an instance of a more general algebraic structure known as a "graph module," which enables the seamless integration of graph-based computations into existing algebraic frameworks. Additionally, we highlight the relevance of GraphBLAS to various machine learning paradigms, including deep learning and randomized algorithms.

Abstract: We consider eigenvalue statistics of large dimensional complex Wishart matrix $W_n$ with independent identically distributed entries, which are not necessarily real or imaginary Gaussian. In particular we study the distribution of its smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{min}(W_n)$ in the limit as n goes to infinity. It turns out that this problem can be reduced to studying the distribution of the largest eigenvalue of a certain Hermitian matrix whose elements depend on those of $W_n$. This allows us to apply the results obtained by Bai (1985) and Bai and Silverstein (2004). As an application, we obtain the limiting distribution of the smallest singular value of a rectangular random matrix with iid entries.

The field of active learning has seen rapid growth and development in recent years, particularly in image segmentation tasks. However, there are still significant challenges that remain to be addressed, one such challenge being uncertainty estimation. In this paper, we propose an approach to active learning based on Bayesian optimization, incorporating both pixel-wise and object-level uncertainties into the model selection process. Our new method uses importance sampling methods and novel ways of estimating epistemic uncertainty to select informative samples from high risk regions that aid convergence towards improved models. We also explore different types of regularization techniques for smoothing the function that relates predicted mask boundaries and label probabilities. Results show our method consistently outperforms standard methods on benchmark datasets by using a combination of these approaches to improve its ability to estimate uncertainty during querying.

In this paper, we present a general framework for complex network-based image segmentation. This approach leverages the principles of networks and graph theory to build efficient and effective algorithms that can accurately perform image segmentation tasks. We begin by introducing some relevant concepts from network analysis, such as nodes, edges, neighborhoods, centrality measures, and subgraph structures. Then, we review various existing techniques in network-based image processing, focusing on their strengths, weaknesses, and challenges. Afterward, we propose our novel algorithmic framework, which integrates several advanced methods from computer vision, machine learning, and graph theory, and can process large scale images with high accuracy. Finally, we illustrate our proposed framework through some experiments and demonstrate its effectiveness among other state of the art approaches.

> Medical imaging modalities, including Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), Computed Tomography (CT) and Ultrasound (US), have different image appearances (e.g., contrast and resolution) due to the underlying physics of image acquisition.

> Thus, domain adaptation (DA) techniques are desirable to adapt a pre-trained model on a high-quality image modality (source modality) to another low-quality image modality (target modality).
>
>
> In this paper, we propose a novel method that first improves the quality of the source modality's image appearance via feature adaptation and then utilizes the image-adapted features to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) for the target modality directly.
> The proposed image-adapted features, in addition to being semantically relevant, are consistent in pixel spatial alignment and resolution.
> Unlike most of the existing methods that conduct DA at either feature-level or pixel-level, ours is a hybrid method targeting both.

>
> Our method synergistically combines these two directions and is capable of learning a set of feature transformation matrices and mapping these matrices to CNN filters based on the modality affinity matrix.
> We use our proposed method to map CT modalities of 17 different anatomical sites to their corresponding US or MRI modalities.

In this paper we present a framework for the automatic estimation of the conditional distribution of an image using iterative inference. The first step is to compute the latent segmentation model, with a score distribution and its respective weights. Our model has two layers. In the first one, we represent both image features and score as an input parameter that are computed for each image and passed to the hidden layer. The model is then used to form a random projection matrix on the class variable and predicts the image in the hidden layer, a process that is known to be slow. At the end of the process, the latent segmentation model is estimated with our training data, and each image is mapped to the hidden layer. The latter is used to generate the map to visualize the latent segmentation result.

In recent years, deep learning methods have gained significant attention in the field of semantic image segmentation due to their ability to learn rich feature representations from large amounts of data. However, applying these methods in real-time applications remains a challenge due to computational complexity and memory constraints.

This survey provides an overview of recent advances in deep learning methods for semantic image segmentation in real-time, focusing on techniques that reduce computational cost while maintaining accuracy. We discuss various architectures, including lightweight networks, knowledge distillation, and efficient inference strategies. Additionally, we explore the use of hardware acceleration, such as GPUs and TPUs, to further improve performance.

Our survey highlights state-of-the-art methods that achieve high accuracy with real-time performance, making them suitable for applications like autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging. We also discuss open challenges and future research directions, including the need for better trade-offs between accuracy and speed, the importance of data quality and diversity, and the potential of transfer learning for domain adaptation.

Overall, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of deep learning methods for semantic image segmentation in real-time, serving as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working in this area.

Abstract Hierarchical image peeling (HIP) is an effective method to extract information about objects in images, but it has been difficult to scale this technique up to large datasets. We present HIP as a flexible framework that can be used to perform hierarchical image filtering on large data sets. The framework consists of two components: a low-level filter and a high-level filter. The low-level filter performs a linear transformation between input and output images, while the high-level filter performs a nonlinear transformation between input and output images. By using these filters, we were able to achieve a significant improvement over previous approaches by reducing the number of parameters required to train the model. Our results show that HIP outperforms other methods such as convolutional neural networks, deep learning, and support vector machines.

The paper "Game characterizations and lower cones in the Weihrauch degrees" presents a novel approach to studying the Weihrauch degrees, a fundamental concept in the field of computational complexity theory. The authors propose a new method based on game-theoretic tools and techniques, which allows for a more fine-grained analysis of the Weihrauch degrees and their properties.

The paper begins by introducing the basic concepts and definitions of the Weihrauch degrees, and then presents a brief overview of the current state of the art in this area. The authors then introduce their new method, which is based on the idea of using games to characterize the Weihrauch degrees. They show how this approach can be used to prove new lower bounds on the Weihrauch degrees of various problems, and how it can be used to separate the Weihrauch degrees of different problems.

The authors then turn their attention to the study of lower cones in the Weihrauch degrees. They show how their game-theoretic approach can be used to prove new results about the structure of lower cones, and how it can be used to solve several longstanding open problems in this area. They also explore the connections between their results and other areas of computer science, such as proof theory and functional programming.

The paper ends with a discussion of the implications of the authors' results, and suggestions for future research directions. Overall, the paper provides a significant new contribution to the study of the Weihrauch degrees, and demonstrates the power and flexibility of the game-theoretic approach to computational complexity theory.

A thin layer of fluid forms around the gas, which grows laterally as it rises due to buoyancy; it then thickens by self-induced flow in the bulk fluid driven via Rayleigh-Taylor instability growth of surface waves on its upper free boundary. In this paper, we present the design and experimental demonstration of a broadband and energy-concentrating terahertz coherent perfect absorber (CPA) based on a self-complementary metasurface. The proposed CPA exploits the concept of self-complementation to achieve high absorption efficiency across a wide range of frequencies, while also concentrating the absorbed energy within a small area.

The designed metasurface consists of a array of asymmetric split-ring resonators that are arranged in a self-complementary pattern, which enables the structure to exhibit both electric and magnetic resonances. By carefully designing the geometry and arrangement of the resonators, we demonstrate that the CPA can achieve high absorption efficiencies exceeding 90% over a bandwidth of more than 30% of the center frequency.

In addition, we show that the CPA can concentrate the absorbed energy within a small area, leading to a significant increase in the power density. This property makes it suitable for various applications such as thermal imaging, non-destructive testing, and wireless power transfer.

Experimental results using a prototype CPA fabricated using standard printed circuit board technology confirm the theoretical predictions and demonstrate the broadband and energy-concentrating properties of the proposed CPA. The measured absorbance spectrum shows high absorption efficiency across a wide frequency range, and the spatial distribution of the absorbed power confirms the concentration of energy within a small area.

Our work presents a significant advancement in the field of THz coherent perfect absorbers, and paves the way for the development of novel devices with enhanced performance and functionality. The proposed CPA has great potential for various practical applications, including THz imaging, sensing, and communication systems.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for solving optimal stopping problems using deep learning techniques. Optimal stopping problems involve finding the best time to stop a process or take a decision in order to maximize a reward signal. They are widely encountered in various fields such as finance, operations research, and machine learning.

Traditional methods for solving optimal stopping problems include dynamic programming, which can be computationally expensive and intractable for large problems. In recent years, there has been growing interest in using machine learning algorithms to solve these problems. However, most of these approaches rely on simplistic models that fail to capture the complex dependencies between the state variables and the reward function.

In this work, we propose a deep learning framework called DeepRank that leverages ranking response surfaces (RRS) to model the relationship between the state variables and the reward function. RRS is a generalization of traditional response surfaces that allows for non-linear and non-monotonic relationships. We use deep neural networks to learn the parameters of the RRS model from data, allowing us to efficiently optimize the stopping policy.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and solution quality. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to various real-world applications, including online advertising and clinical trials.

Our main contributions are:

* A novel deep learning approach for solving optimal stopping problems based on ranking response surfaces
* An efficient algorithm for training the proposed model using off-policy learning
* Thorough evaluation of our method on several benchmark datasets and real-world applications
* Demonstration of the superiority of our approach over existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and solution quality.

Overall, our work provides a promising direction for solving optimal stopping problems using deep learning techniques and opens up new possibilities for tackling complex decision-making problems in various domains.

This research paper critically evaluates a unique, stable method that incorporates Multiscale Petrov-Galerkin (MPG) for the highly oscillatory acoustic scattering problem. The paper starts with presenting issues arising in the traditional Finite Element Method while solving high frequency acoustic scattering problems. We then introduce our theory of the multiscale method, detailing the scheme that makes MPG more efficient and stable than existing methods, especially for high-frequency regimes. Implementations of MPG into two-dimensional problems are provided with extensive numerical examples to demonstrate its stability and effectiveness as a tool for tackling high oscillatory issues. Our research indicates that not only does MPG maintain accuracy, but it also minimizes computational cost compared to traditional methods. This paper will contribute towards increasing understanding and applications of MPG in the field of acoustic scattering. The results may hold significant implications for future research.

Brain tumor detection is a challenging task in medical imaging, as tumors can have varying shapes, sizes, and locations. In this paper, we propose a novel method for brain tumor detection based on bilateral symmetry information. Our approach utilizes a combination of local and global symmetry measures to identify regions of interest in the image, which are then analyzed for the presence of tumors. We evaluate our method on a dataset of MRI images and show that it achieves high accuracy in detecting brain tumors, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our approach provides a valuable tool for clinicians and researchers in the field of brain tumor detection and diagnosis.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic image segmentation called Locally Adaptive Learning Loss (LALL). Semantic image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves assigning class labels to each pixel in an image. Traditional approaches to this problem rely on manually designed loss functions that are applied uniformly across the entire image. However, these losses often fail to capture the complex spatial relationships between classes and can result in suboptimal performance.

Our proposed method addresses this limitation by introducing a locally adaptive learning loss function that varies spatially across the image. The loss function is learned during training and takes into account the local properties of the image, such as the class distribution and boundary locations. This allows the model to focus its learning efforts on regions of the image where accurate segmentation is most important.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it significantly outperforms traditional loss functions. In particular, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC dataset, with an absolute increase in mIoU of X%. We also perform experiments to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our method and provide insights into how they contribute to improved segmentation accuracy.

The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

* Introduction of a locally adaptive learning loss function for semantic image segmentation
* Demonstration of superior performance on several benchmark datasets compared to traditional loss functions
* Analysis of the effectiveness of different components of the proposed method

Overall, our proposed method represents significant progress towards improving the accuracy of semantic image segmentation models. It has broad applications in various domains such as robotics, autonomous driving, medical imaging, video surveillance, and more.

Title: Network Structure of Phonographic Market with Characteristic Similarities between Musicians

Abstract:
The phonographic market refers to the production, distribution, and consumption of recordings and music in a particular time and place. In this paper, we present an overview of the network structure of the phonographic market, with a focus on musicians who have similarities in their popular appeal and creative approaches. The phonographic market is a complex and dynamic network, consisting of agents such as musicians, record labels, distributors, and consumers. Musicians are connected to each other based on their collaborations, tours, and other forms of engagement in the music scene.

We analyze the network structure of the phonographic market using network analysis algorithms such as Degree Distribution, Centrality Analysis, and Group analysis. We find that the musician network in the phonographic market follows a power law distribution, suggesting that musicians’ popularity is highly skewed. This implies that a small group of musicians dominate the scene and have a significant influence on other musicians and the music industry.

We also find significant similarities between musicians in terms of their genre, sub-genre, and musical style. These similarities suggest that musicians in the phonographic market tend to form clusters or groups based on shared characteristics, such as genre, sub-genre, and musical style. These clusters are connected to other clusters through collaborations and other forms of engagement in the music industry.

Finally, we present some implications of our findings, including the potential for personalized recommendations for music consumers and insights into the social dynamics of the music industry. We also suggest avenues for future research and the importance of considering network structure in analyzing the operations of the phonographic market, as well as its role in cultural production.

Segmentation of medical images is a crucial task that helps in various diagnoses and treatment plans. However, achieving accurate segmentation is a challenging task. Human error plays a significant role in segmentation errors. The ground truth is a measure of the accuracy of segmentation, but it requires manual labeling, which is time-consuming and expensive. This paper presents a novel method for disentangling human error from the ground truth in segmentation of medical images. The proposed method uses a deep learning model to estimate segmentation masks, and the ground truth is estimated from the model’s outputs. The human error is estimated by comparing the output masks with the reference masks generated from the model. The results show a significant improvement in estimating the ground truth from model outputs, which can reduce the time and cost required for manual ground truth labeling. The proposed method can help in improving the accuracy of medical image segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a few-shot 3D multi-modal medical image segmentation method using generative adversarial learning. The proposed method can segment an organ from a 3D medical image with only a few annotated images. To our knowledge, this is the first few-shot 3D medical image segmentation method. The proposed method consists of two parts: a generator and a discriminator. The generator is trained to generate fake images that are similar to the real images. The discriminator is trained to distinguish between the fake images and the real images. The generator and the discriminator are trained alternately. The generator is trained to fool the discriminator, and the discriminator is trained to not be fooled by the generator. The training process is repeated until the generator converges. The proposed method is evaluated on the Liver Tumor Segmentation Challenge (LiTS) dataset. The results show that the proposed method can segment the liver from 3D CT images with only a few annotated images.

In the design and implementation of complex systems, component communication is a crucial aspect that affects the overall performance, reliability, and maintainability of the system. There are two main communication paradigms used in component-based systems: synchronous and asynchronous communication. Synchronous communication involves blocking the sender until the receiver responds, while asynchronous communication allows the sender to continue processing without waiting for the receiver's response.

This paper investigates the compatibility properties of synchronously and asynchronously communicating components in terms of their performance, reliability, and maintainability. We evaluate the impact of communication paradigms on the overall system behavior and identify the conditions under which each paradigm is more suitable.

Our results show that synchronous communication is more suitable for systems that require low latency and high throughput, while asynchronous communication is more appropriate for systems that require high scalability and fault tolerance. We also identify the challenges and limitations of each communication paradigm and propose strategies for addressing them.

The paper contributes to the understanding of component communication and its impact on system design and implementation. The findings and insights provided in this paper can help system designers and developers make informed decisions when choosing the appropriate communication paradigm for their systems.

Keywords: component communication, synchronous communication, asynchronous communication, performance, reliability, maintainability, compatibility properties.

In this paper, the authors investigate the structure and morphology of epitaxially grown Fe3O4/NiO bilayers on MgO(001) substrates using a combination of characterization techniques including X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and scanning transmission electron microscopy. They find that the Fe3O4 layer grows in a cubic spinel structure and is epitaxially aligned with the MgO substrate, while the NiO layer forms a rock-salt structure with an interface layer between NiO and Fe3O4. The morphology of the bilayers is found to be highly dependent on growth conditions, with varying degrees of surface roughness and island formation observed. Overall, the results provide valuable insights into the structural properties of these Fe3O4/NiO bilayers, which are important for potential applications in spintronics and magnetic storage devices.

This paper presents a study on the directional infrared emission resulting from cascade population inversion and four-wave mixing in Rb vapours. The authors investigate the effects of cascade population inversion on the four-wave mixing process in Rb vapours, which leads to the generation of directional infrared emission. The study is conducted using a diode-pumped solid-state (DPSS) laser and a high-resolution spectrometer. The results show that the directional infrared emission is strongly dependent on the cascade population inversion and the four-wave mixing process. The authors also discuss the potential applications of this phenomenon in the field of optical communication and sensing.

The field of medical image segmentation has seen significant advancements in recent years, with deep learning techniques such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, these methods often struggle to handle complex and high-dimensional data, leading to slow training times and limited accuracy. In this study, we propose a novel approach to address these challenges by using thickened 2D networks for efficient 3D medical image segmentation. Our method involves applying multiple thin layers of CNNs sequentially to each slice of the input image, resulting in a more robust and accurate model that can effectively handle large amounts of data. We demonstrate our approach on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of both speed and accuracy. Overall, our work represents an important step towards developing scalable and effective solutions for medical image segmentation tasks.

The brain is extremely complex and dense; we cannot estimate at the individual level all its spatial and temporal parameters, nor the number of neurons distributed in the cortex. Despite this, the largest existing dataset still does not offer sufficient details to make reliable judgments about the brain. We investigate a new method for segmenting a single neuronal population in a voxelwise manner by using a fully connected perceptron network. While a previous study by [Shi et al., 2011], [Jee et al., 2015] employed a similar method, this is the first time that fully convolutional deep neural networks, instead of conventional activation function or convolutional architectures are used. Unlike the previous study, which used convolutional networks specifically for segmenting brain tissue, we apply these convolutions with regularization terms to enhance the generalization performance, thereby ensuring sufficient computational resource. Thus, we use the method for segmenting an entire brain from the voxel-wise perspective, and we evaluate its performance in both static and dynamic (i.e., dynamic sensing) scenarios.

In this paper, we propose a new challenge called VisDA: The Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge. The goal of VisDA is to evaluate the ability of machine learning models to adapt to changes in the visual domain, specifically when encountering unseen data from different domains or environments.

Domain adaptation has become an increasingly important research area due to its potential applications in various fields such as computer vision, robotics, and autonomous driving. However, most existing work focuses on adapting models to new environments within the same domain (e.g., adapting a model trained on synthetic images to real-world images). There is a lack of benchmarks and challenges that test a model's ability to generalize across multiple domains with diverse visual styles, modalities, and formats.

To address this gap, we introduce VisDA, which consists of several tasks that require participants to develop models that can adapt to various visual domain shifts. These tasks include image classification, object detection, segmentation, and generation, each with their own set of source and target datasets representing different domains. We also provide a comprehensive evaluation framework to measure the performance of participating models under different domain shift scenarios.

The paper presents details of the VisDA challenge, including dataset descriptions, task definitions, evaluation metrics, and submission guidelines. We invite researchers and practitioners from academia and industry to participate in VisDA and contribute solutions that advance the state-of-the-art in visual domain adaptation. The challenge will be hosted annually, with results published in a dedicated proceedings volume at top AI conferences. By fostering a community-driven effort towards solving this critical problem, we envision VisDA to play a vital role in catalyzing innovations that enable more robust and reliable AI systems for real-world applications.

Discrete-time quantum walks (DTQW) have been shown to be capable of traversing obstacles that classical random walks cannot. We find that the traversal of narrow bottlenecks is determined by the internal degrees of freedom of the quantum walker, which distinguishes it from classical walkers. We observe traversal in configurations that are unattainable for classical particles, including walkers that are thinner than the bottleneck. Furthermore, we find a novel type of crossover in a parameter range that is inaccessible to classical particles, which is characterized by the dominance of the internal degrees of freedom of the walker. Our results indicate that quantum systems can display a richer set of behaviours than classical systems, which is relevant to applications in quantum technologies.
